name: Pentecostalism
notes: Azusa Street in 1906 is the principal timeline marker here, while Topeka in 1901 and older Holiness roots preceded it. This is a diverse worldwide movement, not a single body founded only in Los Angeles.
summary: A diverse Christian movement emphasizing present experience of the Holy Spirit and the continuation of spiritual gifts.
formation_narrative: Pentecostal revival grew from several evangelical and Holiness environments. Charles Parham’s Topeka circle in 1901 and William Seymour’s Azusa Street revival from 1906 became influential American centers, but no single institution founded every global Pentecostal stream. Some older Holiness churches later adopted Pentecostal teaching. Trinitarian and Oneness traditions, and Wesleyan and Finished Work accounts of sanctification, demonstrate the movement’s internal diversity.
core_beliefs: Spirit baptism and gifts: participants expect the Spirit’s activity in testimony, tongues, healing, and mission.
Experiential faith: biblical teaching is connected with conversion, prayer, and recognizable spiritual experience.
Diversity of doctrine: not all Pentecostals share one account of sanctification or the Trinity, so a denominational statement cannot function as a universal movement creed.

name: Assemblies of God
notes: The 1914 date is for the US General Council. Its relationship to the World Assemblies of God Fellowship and national churches must be distinguished; the inherited global membership range is not a verified US membership total.
summary: A Pentecostal fellowship whose American General Council was organized in 1914 for mission, doctrinal fellowship, and ministerial support.
formation_narrative: Ministers gathered at Hot Springs, Arkansas, to coordinate a rapidly expanding Pentecostal network. E. N. Bell and J. Roswell Flower were elected early officers. The adoption of the Statement of Fundamental Truths in 1916 clarified a Trinitarian doctrinal basis. The United States body is part of a wider world fellowship of national organizations; global membership should not be mistaken for membership of the American General Council.
core_beliefs: Trinitarian faith: the statement affirms one God as Father, Son, and Spirit, distinguishing this fellowship from Oneness Pentecostal bodies.
Spirit baptism: a further empowering experience is associated with speaking in tongues as initial physical evidence.
Mission and healing: evangelism, prayer for healing, and expectation of Christ’s return shape its understanding of ministry.

name: Church of God (Cleveland, Tennessee)
summary: A Holiness-Pentecostal denomination tracing its institutional roots to an 1886 Christian Union in Tennessee.
formation_narrative: Richard Green Spurling and a small community organized a Christian Union in 1886 seeking New Testament fellowship. Later Holiness revival and Pentecostal experience changed its religious life; the name Church of God was adopted in 1907. Under A. J. Tomlinson the movement expanded organization and mission. Its 1886 foundation therefore precedes the 1906 Azusa marker used for the Pentecostal movement node.
core_beliefs: Sanctification: the church teaches sanctification after justification, expressing its Wesleyan-Holiness ancestry.
Spirit baptism and gifts: its commitments affirm Spirit baptism with tongues and the continuing activity of spiritual gifts.
Practical discipleship: biblical teaching, holy living, worship, and evangelism are held together rather than treated as unrelated practices.

name: Church of God in Christ
notes: The COGIC name dates to 1897; Mason’s Pentecostal turn and the division with Jones occurred in 1907. The exact national-convention parent and a precise 1896 separation need stronger evidence.
summary: A historically Black Holiness-Pentecostal denomination whose 1890s formation preceded its adoption of Pentecostal teaching in 1907.
formation_narrative: Charles Harrison Mason and Charles Price Jones worked in a Holiness revival setting after conflict with Baptist churches. The Church of God in Christ name dates to 1897. Mason’s 1907 visit to Azusa Street and his acceptance of Pentecostal teaching led to a division with Jones. Mason’s followers retained the COGIC name and built an episcopally organized church with national institutions in Memphis.
core_beliefs: Conversion and sanctification: repentance, faith, and the Spirit’s renewing work should produce a holy life.
Pentecostal experience: Spirit baptism is sought by believers, with healing and spiritual empowerment central to the published faith statement.
Trinitarian and biblical confession: the church affirms one God in three persons and Scripture as its written doctrinal norm.

name: Foursquare Church
notes: Developed from McPherson’s evangelistic ministry and Angelus Temple in 1923; incorporation steps followed in 1927. A direct institutional split from Assemblies of God has not been established by the authoritative history consulted.
summary: A Pentecostal church family that developed from Aimee Semple McPherson’s evangelistic ministry and Angelus Temple.
formation_narrative: McPherson established Los Angeles as a base for evangelism, opened Angelus Temple in 1923, and developed training, church planting, radio, and overseas mission. Incorporation steps followed in 1927 after a wider network had formed. Its name expresses a fourfold presentation of Jesus. Personal connections with other Pentecostal ministries do not by themselves prove that the entire body was created by an institutional split from the Assemblies of God.
core_beliefs: Jesus as Savior: salvation through Christ is the first element of the fourfold message.
Jesus as Spirit baptizer and healer: Pentecostal empowerment and prayer for healing are prominent in its teaching.
Jesus as coming King: expectation of Christ’s return completes the fourfold scheme and motivates mission.
